title: How Financial Advisors Can Ask Clients for Referrals
summary: Asking for referrals can be an effective way to gain new leads through existing clients, but it's important to know the right way to do it.
body_markdown:
> Asking clients for[referrals](https://smartasset.com/advisor-resources/best-referral-sources-for-financial-advisors-2023) starts with choosing the right clients, recognizing when they’re happiest with your service and making the request feel like a conversation rather than a pitch. That sounds simple, yet only 51% of registered investment advisors proactively ask for referrals, according to a 2026 Cerulli Edge report.1 Many worry it will feel awkward or transactional. This guide covers whom to ask, how to set the tone and timing, which approach to use and sample referral request letters you can adapt.

## **How to Ask Clients for Referrals**


Asking for referrals can be tricky if you’re attempting it for the first time. You may worry about sounding too forward, which is natural. Developing a framework and system for asking for referrals can help you feel confident and your clients feel comfortable as you navigate these conversations.


Here are some tips to remember as you ask clients for referrals:


### Decide Who to Ask


Every client is different, and some may be more open to the idea of referring you to people in their circle than others. Likewise, some clients may have a broader circle of connections who align with your[ideal client profile](https://smartasset.com/advisor-resources/ideal-client-profile-for-financial-advisors) .


If you’ve segmented your book of business, that may offer valuable clues about which clients to ask for referrals. For example, are there any clients who already refer prospects to you consistently? Or, do you have clients who work in fields that bring them into contact with the type of people who are a match for your services? You may also view your book through the assets under management lens if you’re hoping to[attract more high-net-worth clients](https://smartasset.com/advisor-resources/how-to-attract-high-net-worth-clients) .


Make a list (or multiple lists) of clients who appear most promising as referral sources. Then, use what you know about each one to rate their receptiveness to a referral request, and how likely they are to follow through. If your list is short, consider whether you need to learn more about your clients’ networks, clarify whom you can help or gather feedback about their experience with your firm.


### Strike the Right Tone


When asking for referrals, what you’re really asking your clients for is a favor. Keep the tone polite and friendly, and project confidence. Be respectful and acknowledge that referrals are not a requirement to be your client. While it may be tempting to develop a fixed speech, your clients may be able to tell if you’re reading from a[script](https://smartasset.com/advisor-resources/cold-calling-scripts-for-financial-advisors) .


Opt for authenticity and allow the conversation to flow naturally. Show your gratitude and be specific in communicating how you might be able to help their friends or family members strengthen their financial plans. Your clients shouldn’t feel pressured to refer you; your messaging should let them know that referrals are certainly appreciated, but always optional.


### Be Mindful of Timing


Timing can have an impact on the success of your referral requests. A client who’s just experienced a 10% portfolio drop, for example, may not be the best person to ask for a referral if they chalk the loss up to your investment advice.


A natural time to ask for a referral is when clients are most satisfied with the service they’re receiving. If you’re unsure how your clients feel, you might ask them to complete a short[experience survey](https://smartasset.com/advisor-resources/client-survey-questions-for-financial-advisors) . At the end, you could include this question: *On a scale of 1 to 5, where 1 means unlikely and 5 means very likely, how likely are you to refer this advisory firm to friends and family?*


Your clients’ responses can shed light on where satisfaction may be lacking. Once the survey response window closes, you might send a follow-up survey asking clients to share additional thoughts on what’s preventing them from being fully satisfied. Critique may be difficult to hear initially, but it can be exceptionally valuable in improving the advisor-client relationship so that when you do ask for referrals, the response is a positive one.


### Choose an Ask Method


You’ll also need to give some thought to how you want to ask for referrals. You might make your request in person when meeting with clients, via email or text, or though direct mail campaigns.


If you’re planning to ask for referrals when concluding a client meeting, keep it short and simple. You can use one of the talking points from the meeting as a springboard for the request.


For example, say that you’ve just been discussing legacy and[estate planning](https://smartasset.com/advisor-resources/how-to-get-estate-planning-clients) with one of your clients. As they’re preparing to leave, you might say something along these lines:


*“I’m glad we had a chance to go over some of your concerns about passing on wealth today. I understand how that can be stressful. And if you know anyone who’s going through a similar situation, I’d be happy to chat with them to help put their mind at ease.”*


You don’t have to use that exact wording; this is just an example. But dropping the request into the conversation casually might prompt them to mentally scan their list of friends and family for anyone who might need your services.


The same approach can work for email and direct mail referral requests. What you’re missing with these requests is the opportunity to gauge a client’s initial reaction to asking for referrals since they’re not in front of you. If you decide to send any type of referral request communication to clients, consider how it should be worded for[compliance](https://smartasset.com/advisor-resources/ria-compliance-checklist) .

## **Sample Client Referral Request**


Writing a client referral request letter can take a little time as you want to ensure that you’re getting the format and messaging right. Here are a few tips to keep in mind as you write your letter:


- Personalize the message by referencing something unique to the client, such as a recent issue you helped them with or a shared personal/professional connection.
- Keep it brief and to the point; don’t let your referral request get lost in an overly wordy note.
- Be specific about what you’re asking for but keep the tone polite, not overbearing.
- Thank the client for considering the request and mention that you’re looking forward to your next meeting.


Here’s what a sample client referral request letter might look like:


---


Dear \[Client Name\],


This is just a quick note to say hello and follow up on the changes to your investment plan we discussed at our last meeting. It’s important that you feel comfortable with the solutions being offered and confident about the results you’re seeing. Your satisfaction is always a top priority.


If someone in your circle has questions about their financial plan or is looking for an advisor, I’d be happy to have an introductory conversation. You’re welcome to share my contact information, with no obligation.


Looking forward to our next meeting,


\[Your Name\]


---


You can tweak this, of course, but it should give you an idea of what to include when asking clients for referrals. You’re underscoring the value you provide to them, reminding them that you’re always there if they need you and gently prompting them to tell their friends and family members about you.


The client may or may not respond; in some cases, a referral may be the response. If a client does refer someone to you, it’s good to[follow up](https://smartasset.com/advisor-resources/financial-advisor-follow-up-email) with a brief thank you note. Here’s an example of what that might look like:


---


Dear \[Client Name\],


Thank you for referring \[Prospect Name\] to me. I’m looking forward to building our relationship. I appreciate you taking the time to tell them about me, and I hope I can continue to exceed your expectations as we work together.


Regards,


\[Your Name\]


---

## Why Is Asking for Referrals Important?


There are many ways to attract new clients to your business, but referrals can be one of the most effective. With a built-in network of potential prospects, all you need to do is tap into the connections you already have.


When clients refer friends, family, or colleagues, it’s a strong testament to their trust in your services. Satisfied clients are more likely to recommend you, generating valuable leads and contributing to long-term business growth.


[Client referrals](https://smartasset.com/advisor-resources/financial-advisor-referrals) act as a form of free advertising, and word-of-mouth can be incredibly powerful. If you’re not actively seeking referrals, you may be missing out on valuable opportunities to connect with new clients and expand your business.

## Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)


**Can Financial Advisors Pay for Referrals?**


[Advisors can pay for referrals](https://smartasset.com/advisor-resources/can-financial-advisors-pay-referral-fees) , though they’ll need to observe compliance rules to do so. Whether it makes sense to pay for referrals depends on the type of clientele you serve, and how likely they are to refer prospects to you organically.


**How Can Advisors Build a Strong Referral Program?**


Advisors can[build a strong referral program](https://smartasset.com/advisor-resources/financial-advisor-referral-program) by defining what counts as a referral, including a strong incentive for clients and asking for referrals from clients who are most likely to be responsive. Developing a system for tracking how many referrals you receive, how many of those referrals book a call and how many eventually convert can help you gauge how well your program is working.


**How Can Advisors Ask for Referrals From Their Network?**


Advisors may tap their networks to[build centers of influence](https://smartasset.com/advisor-resources/centers-of-influence) consisting of attorneys, insurance agents, accountants, bankers and other financial services professionals. These individuals may refer prospective clients with no direct ask required if they understand the advisor’s value and service offerings. Cultivating relationships with centers of influence and consistently demonstrating value could increase this type of referral traffic.


## **Bottom Line**


Asking for referrals can feel more comfortable when requests are specific, well timed and optional. A consistent process for identifying potential referral sources, making requests and thanking clients can help you build on existing relationships and evaluate what generates new introductions.
